To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

multiplex ligation- dependent probe amplification (a technique that detects deletions and duplications of whole exons) uncovers large genomic DCX deletions in 3 of the 11 women (all with anterior gradient of migration) with band heterotopia in whom no DCX mutations were found after sequencing.

multiplex ligation- dependent probe amplification detects large deletions of the double cortin gene, which are a frequent cause of subcortical band (double) heterotopia, in patients with normal gene sequencing.
multiplex ligation- dependent probe amplification ( MLPA) detects DCX gene exonic deletions in bandheterotopia.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the genetic basis of a brain developmental disorder called band heterotopia, which is caused by a defect in neuronal migration, and which results in a double cortex, a condition in which the brain has two layers of gray matter.
the development of a new technique, called multiplex ligation dependent probe amplification, to detect deletions of DCX gene in patients with SBH.
the identification of a new genetic cause of SBH, which will help to improve the genetic counseling of patients with this condition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
65% to 80% of SBH cases harbor mutations of the DCX or FLNA genes, depending on the population studied.

65% (15 of 23) of patients with sporadic SBH and an A>P gradient have a DCX mutation, and that MLPA should be used to search for DCX mutations in all cases of SBH in which gene sequencing is negative.

DCX gene mutations (including deletions) are present in 65% of women with sporadic SBH, 53% of women with diffuse SBH, 100% of women with anteriorly predominant SB, 0% of women with posteriorly predominant SBH, and 0% of men with sporadic or posteriorly predominant SB.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the DCX gene mutations account for 65% of SBH in women and for 100% of SBH when the mutation is present in the father and transmitted to the daughter.
DCX mutations account for 65% of cases of sporadic SBH, and that the DCX gene is deleted in 5% of cases.
the DCX gene mutations are found in 65% of patients with SBX.
The main takeaway from our work is that
DCX deletions are an underascertainment of SBH.
MLPA should be used as a second-tier test in patients with SBH and no mutation detected by gene sequencing.
the DCX gene can be affected by deletions that encompass one or several exons.
